descriptors.concept_name: Rule of Majority and Foundation of Oppression Concept
descriptors.definition: The rule of majority dictates that corporate decisions made by the majority shareholding must be respected, limiting judicial intervention in internal company matters. This governance principle creates vulnerabilities where minority shareholders can be legally sidelined, necessitating specific statutory protections against oppression and mismanagement.
inclusion: Majoritarian corporate governance principles
Historical legal precedents on internal management
Basic rationale for legislative intervention in corporate disputes
exclusion: Specific statutory eligibility thresholds for filing tribunal petitions
Detailed remedial orders issued by judicial authorities
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from statutory minority relief applications which provide exceptions to the general non-interference stance of majority rule.

descriptors.concept_name: Application To Tribunal For Relief In Cases Of Oppression, Etc. [Section 241]
descriptors.definition: Eligible members or the Central Government can apply to the Tribunal alleging that corporate affairs are conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest, company interests, or oppressive to members. Additionally, complaints may target material management or structural changes that threaten future prejudicial conduct.
inclusion: Member applications regarding oppressive conduct
Central Government applications
Complaints concerning prejudicial management changes
exclusion: Direct shareholder class actions under separate statutory provisions
General winding up proceedings initiated independently of oppression claims
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from general corporate governance disputes by requiring demonstrable prejudice or oppression to members, public interest, or the company.

descriptors.definition: Section 244 prescribes specific membership thresholds and eligibility criteria required for members to maintain a petition under Section 241. The Tribunal holds discretionary power to waive these statutory requirements upon application to ensure genuine grievances can be addressed.
inclusion: Minimum member count or shareholding requirements for companies with share capital
Proportional membership requirements for companies without share capital
Tribunal powers to waive eligibility thresholds
exclusion: Substantive remedial powers of the Tribunal over corporate management
Class action proceedings governed by separate statutory rules
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from the substantive grounds for oppression under Section 241 by focusing strictly on the procedural standing and qualification of petitioners.

descriptors.definition: The Tribunal is vested with extensive judicial powers to issue remedial orders when it finds oppression, mismanagement, or prejudice, provided winding up would unfairly punish the aggrieved members. These permissible measures include regulating future company conduct, altering management agreements, and restructuring share capital.
inclusion: Orders regulating future affairs
Share purchase directions and capital reductions
Modification or termination of managerial agreements
exclusion: Initial procedural qualification checks for filing petitions
Penal provisions resulting from contravening subsequent modification rules
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from preliminary petition filing rules by representing the actual discretionary remedies applied post-adjudication.

descriptors.concept_name: Consequences Of Termination Or Modification Of Certain Agreements [Section 243]
descriptors.definition: When the Tribunal modifies or terminates corporate agreements under statutory powers, affected managers lose entitlement to compensation or damages for loss of office. Furthermore, such individuals are disqualified from holding managerial positions in any company for five years without prior Tribunal leave.
inclusion: Statutory bar on claiming compensation for terminated contracts
Five-year managerial appointment restriction
Penalties for contravening disqualification terms
exclusion: Initial discretionary powers of the Tribunal to issue structural remedies
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from general contract termination rules under civil law by stripping statutory rights to damages and imposing strict executive bans.

descriptors.definition: Section 245 enables shareholders and depositors to institute collective class actions before the Tribunal against companies, directors, auditors, or advisors for prejudicial management or fraudulent acts. Eligible members can seek restraining orders, declare fraudulent alterations void, and claim damages or compensation.
inclusion: Collective petitions by members or depositors
Restraints against ultra vires or unlawful corporate acts
Claims for damages against auditors, experts, and directors
exclusion: Individual member petitions strictly limited to personal oppression claims under Section 241
General winding up and liquidation administrative tasks
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from individual oppression petitions under Section 241 by serving a collective representative function targeting broader corporate governance, auditor, and expert liabilities.

descriptors.concept_name: Application Of Certain Provisions To Proceedings Under Section 241 Or Section 245 [Section 246]
descriptors.definition: Specific statutory provisions concerning winding-up offenses, fraudulent business conduct, and officer liability apply mutatis mutandis to proceedings initiated under Section 241 or Section 245. This ensures that fraudulent applications and delinquent managerial behavior during oppression or class action proceedings face appropriate penalties and damage assessments.
inclusion: Application of winding-up penalty provisions to oppression proceedings
Liability assessment for fraudulent conduct or missing accounts
Extension of liabilities to partners and corporate directors
exclusion: Standard operational management decisions free from fraud or bad faith
nearby_distinctions: Distinguished from standard remedial relief provisions by importing penal liquidation consequences directly into active tribunal litigation for misconduct.
